pass_a_gloss: (consider him made less a little) beside angels, so that we in him may be enriched with the things beyond our own nature in the good pleasure of God and Father; for he raised us together and seated us together in the heavenlies in Christ. For while the Savior of us all, Christ, sits in council (enthroned), the boast will run over the whole nature of man. Since in what way have we been enriched by his poverty, if in no way our condition was in better things when the one above all creation became according to us? He was made less, therefore, a little beside angels, having become man, so that he might honor the nature of man and bring it back again to the condition at the beginnings, being crowned with glory and honor also in it, though being lord of the glory as God. For as the transgression of Adam showed us most dishonored, so we have been glorified through the obedience of Christ on our behalf, he having also laid down his own soul (life) 'so that he may be lord of both dead and living'. (385) How was he made less beside the angels, the one worshiped by them? Or (is it not) that he came down into the measures of humanity, and having taken the body naturally disposed to die he suffered in it willingly, and is crowned with the highest glories through the suffering, as having through it abolished death and shown corruption ineffective, inasmuch as being incorruption and life. And the things of superiority belong to the angels, that both outside flesh and of dying they are superior, the Son having come to be in these things through the voluntary emptying. But the one made less a little beside angels on account of the measure of humanity, being in the superiority of godhead, is worshiped by them, and is enthroned on seats which those stand around always glorifying, and naming him lord of the powers. (386) 'So that by the grace of God he may taste death on behalf of everyone.' What 'he tasted for everyone' (means) is clear, as at least I think. For having given his own body to death and as it were having tasted fleshly of what befell, he came back to life again and trampled at once the might of death. Therefore the one said to have been made less a little beside angels is himself the Word from God, not having suffered the lessening into his own nature; for he is always himself and holding the same way, unturnable and unalterable, but having endured this also for us humanly; for he put up, though being God by nature, with the measures of humanity on account of the economy; and this is of the mystery concerning him the thing most fitting to be marveled at. So also the prophet Habakkuk said 'Lord, I have heard your hearing and I feared, I perceived your works and I was astonished'; for truly an astonishment and beyond every wonder is what has happened. But I do not know how, not having understood the mystery about it rightly, some speak emptily and indeed have also written, wishing to interpret the things in the eighth psalm: 'Let us look then who is the man about whom he is struck and marvels that indeed the Only-begotten deigned both to remember him and to make a visitation.' Then to these he adds, and very clearly, that 'What is man that you remember him, or son of man that you visit him?' is not said of every man, but about the Son alone; and they try to make firm their own words and carry them round into truth, saying that the blessed Paul (took) the things in the psalm to his person, (387) on account of saying 'But the one made less a little beside angels we see, Jesus, through the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor.' Then, separating the natures, they say that the man born from the holy virgin is entirely (a man) individually, about whom also, he says, David marvels, that he has been deemed worthy of both remembrance and visitation; and he has been deemed worthy also of the things beyond his own nature, as being benefited by God the Word. But they have been ignorant, as it seems, that Christ Jesus is not according to himself a man understood and said by us commonly and individually, but rather the Word from God having become man. And so that the rendering of the thoughts (continues).
pass_b_english: than the angels, so that we in him might be enriched with what is beyond our own nature, by the good pleasure of God the Father. For he "raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ" (Ephesians 2:6). Since Christ, the Savior of us all, sits enthroned with the Father, the boast will run through the whole of human nature. Otherwise, how have we been made rich by his poverty (2 Corinthians 8:9), if our condition was in no way raised to something better when the one who is above all creation became one of us? So he was made a little lower than the angels by becoming man, in order to honor the nature of man and to bring it back to what it was at the beginning, being crowned with glory and honor in it as well, though as God he is the Lord of glory. For just as Adam's transgression showed us to be utterly without honor, so we have been glorified through the obedience of Christ on our behalf, who laid down even his own life "so that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living" (Romans 14:9).

How was he made lower than the angels, he who is worshiped by them? Was it not that he came down into the measures of humanity, took a body that by nature dies, and suffered in it willingly; and that he is crowned with the highest glories because of the suffering, as having abolished death through it and made corruption powerless, since he is incorruption and life? The angels' advantage is that they are outside the flesh and above dying, while the Son came to be in these things through his voluntary self-emptying. But the one made a little lower than the angels because of the measure of humanity, being in the supremacy of the Godhead, is worshiped by them, and he is seated on thrones around which they stand, glorifying him always and naming him Lord of the powers.

"So that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone" (Hebrews 2:9). What "he tasted for everyone" means is clear, I think. For he gave his own body to death and, so to speak, tasted in the flesh what befell it; then he came back to life and at once trampled down the power of death. So the one said to have been made a little lower than the angels is the Word who is from God himself. He did not suffer the lessening in his own nature, for he is always himself and the same, unchangeable and unalterable; but he underwent this too for our sake, in a human way. For though he is God by nature, he put up with the measures of humanity for the sake of the economy. And this, in the mystery that concerns him, is what most deserves our wonder. So too the prophet Habakkuk said, "Lord, I have heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was amazed" (Habakkuk 3:2). For what took place is truly an amazement, beyond all wonder. Yet somehow certain people, not having understood the mystery concerning him rightly, talk emptily, and have even written, wanting to interpret what is in the eighth psalm:

"Let us consider, then, who is the man at whom he is astonished and marvels that the Only-begotten deigned to remember him and to visit him." Then to this he adds, and very plainly, that "What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?" (Psalm 8:4) is not said of every man, but of the Son alone. They try to make their own words firm and to pass them off as truth by saying that the blessed Paul applied the words of the psalm to his person, because he says, "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death" (Hebrews 2:9). Then, dividing the natures, they say that the one born of the holy Virgin is wholly a man in his own right; it is at him, they say, that David marvels, that he was thought worthy of remembrance and of visitation, and was thought worthy also of what is beyond his own nature, as one who receives benefits from God the Word. But they have failed to see, it seems, that Christ Jesus is not thought of or spoken of by us as a man by himself, either in the common or in the individual sense, but rather as the Word from God made man.
